title: The Buddha's map of attention
hookLine: a to-do list for attention, four lines long: body, feelings, mind, and what the mind meets
carry: mindfulness looks at body, feelings, mind, dhammas

lines: BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, WHAT THE MIND MEETS.
cards: One of the Buddha's discourses hands its listeners something like a to-do list for attention, four lines long. Not a list of beliefs. A list of places to look.
One: the body. Two: feelings. Three: the mind itself.
Four: the things the mind meets and works with. Each line opens into detailed instructions, and the whole is framed as a path.
Back on day seven hundred sixty-five, this same discourse took us to a charnel ground; today, the whole map.

teach.h: ONE: THE BODY, STARTING WITH BREATH.
teach.b: Satipatthana is the Pali word for these four foundations, or establishings, of mindfulness. The sutta sits in the Middle Length Discourses, number ten. First, the body.
It starts with breathing: a meditator goes to a quiet place, sits, and knows a long breath as long and a short breath as short.

Then it widens to the postures, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and to ordinary actions like eating and dressing, done knowing what you're doing. Second, feelings. Here feeling doesn't mean emotion.
It means the simple tone of an experience: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. The meditator just knows which one is present.

teach.h: THREE: KNOW THE MIND AS IT IS.
teach.b: Third, the mind. Angry or not? Scattered or gathered?
The instruction isn't to fix it; it's to know it as it is.

Fourth, the things the mind meets, in Pali, dhammas. Here the sutta lists teachings to watch in action: hindrances like restlessness and doubt, the factors that lead toward awakening, and the four noble truths.

Through all four runs a refrain, in paraphrase: the meditator watches ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, noticing things arising and passing away. That points straight at tomorrow. Two things worth noticing.
Dogen's just sitting set the techniques down; this sutta lays out a careful map. Different schools, different ways in, each with its own teachers.
And the list starts with breath and body: the abstract parts come last, after you've learned to feel your own feet.

how: In Theravada Buddhism, meditation teachers draw on the Satipatthana Sutta, and students practice mindfulness of breath and body, feeling tones, states of mind and the teachings as they show up in experience.

games.q: you sit, and notice the moment feels unpleasant. following the second foundation, what's the move?
o: change something until it feels pleasant.
just know it: this is unpleasant.
skip ahead to the fourth foundation.
games.why: the sutta asks the meditator just to know which tone is present: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither.

practice: Give each foundation about half a minute: feel one breath, long or short, and where you touch the chair; then ask whether this moment is pleasant, unpleasant or neither.
Know whether the mind is busy or quiet, scattered or gathered, without fixing it. Last, notice what it meets, restlessness, doubt or a little calm, and watch it come and change.
